text: Seven o'clock, and instead of dinner, sirens. Out at sea the water glows violet, and the barge is listing.
Branch Chief Yang lets the phone ring and slams the emergency button. Seoul signs his budget, but the harbour comes first.
Every phone in the market lights up with the same order.
Seoa grabs the market's megaphone, and the aunties fall in behind a fifteen-year-old without a word of argument.
Up on a fish crate, she keeps the crowd walking, not running.
On the market roof, Bomi, serious for once, streams the escape routes to three million people.
Then Choi's van screeches in. Invited to dinner, he has brought a healer instead of a side dish.
Yerin jumps down, shaking but ready, the girl who froze in front of a lizard on her first raid.
Seoa shoves him toward the breakwater. She got fourteen people across a falling bridge in Mangwon. She can handle a market.
So they walk out to the neck of the breakwater, where Geum held the line ten years ago.
Three seconds left on the lid.
The lid bursts. Stone slabs the size of buses fly into the sky.
And out of the water come the brine crawlers. Hundreds of them.
Violet motes drift down like snow, and for once that helps: with the sea gate open, his summons recharge in a minute instead of hours.
Two fingers to his temple, Jaeha calls all four by name, then gives the old guild rule. His rule now.
For the first time, all four flare together: amber, moss green, river blue and lilac.
Pim hears the whole swarm and finds the real problem: the left side.
Nib tears through the first wave.
Lyra pins them to the rocks, one arrow after another.
Borro shoves an entire wave back into the sea.
Where she stood ten years ago, Geum swings once, and the whole wave turns to ash, her younger self behind her like a ghost.
On the pier, three old fishermen slowly take off their caps.
Geum is grinning. She's had ten years to pick a name for this thing.
But a second tide is pouring up the market's sea wall toward the crowd, and they're too far away.
Then a truck skids up, and twenty-eight white husks leap off in perfect unison.
Moon Ahin strides out in her white coat-dress and raises her baton like a conductor. For once, she asks for Jaeha's plan.
He wants a husk wall on the sea wall, its weight running through him. Moon Ahin heard Geum's warning. Jaeha calls it fair trade.
As each husk runs past, Moon Ahin touches its shoulder and names it. Her uncle taught her never to.
The husks lock arms along the sea wall, and the swarm breaks against them, every husk linked to Jaeha.
A hundred and sixty percent. Five days of ice raised his limit, but not that far.
His heart starts to stumble.
Geum glances back at him and frowns.
Then the boss surfaces: a back too big to see the end of, rusted plates from the old lid in its hide.
On the barge, the engineers follow the Director's orders.
Four harpoons slam into her back.
And she keeps coming, towing the whole barge behind her like a toy.
The barge runs aground on the breakwater's rocks, and the chains drag her to a stop.
The links carry the farm's stamped mark.
Nib knows those chains. They held his commander.
Nib only has to say it once. Jaeha's answer is instant.
Nib leaps onto the grounded barge and runs straight up a chain, thirty metres above the water.
At each anchor, he hammers out the shackle pin with his knife hilt.
Han Sora takes aim at him with her crossbow, and then lowers it.
The last chains whip free and lash across the barge's deck.
Nib lands back on the tetrapods. Kanghan's second farm is over.
Freed, the Deep Lantern rises over the harbour: an S-grade leviathan, hushed, her lantern burning violet.
Her small, ancient eye finds Jaeha.
The broken voice speaks again, accusing him. Pim understands: she has mistaken Jaeha for the man who stopped.
Her lantern pulses, and violet light washes over the harbour. The only shadow is under her head, so Geum keeps them close.
The crowd stops, turns, and walks back toward the water, eyes glassy. Choi and Yerin grab whoever they can.
And Seoa lowers the megaphone and walks toward the edge of the pier.
Jaeha is two hundred metres away and can't reach her. But Pim can reach all of them.
Pim bounds up a harbour light tower, opens his wings and screams a signal louder than the lantern.
Seoa blinks awake at the edge, and her first move is to haul back a little boy still walking off it.
On Bomi's stream, four million people watch a moth save Busan.
And Seoa, shaking, a boy clinging to her blazer, raises the megaphone again.
Then the Deep Lantern raises a hand fifteen metres wide over the breakwater.
Borro raises his shield, and Geum steps in beside him. One wall won't be enough.
The hand comes down, and they hold it, shield and ladle side by side, the whole crowd behind them.
To keep Borro standing, Jaeha carries him too. Twenty-nine at once. Blood runs from his nose and his ears.
The warning window glitches and tears: the heart Geum warned him about.
The world starts to go grey.
From under the hand, Geum shouts the ending she never told him: that man didn't choose to stop. His body gave out.
On his knees and bleeding, Jaeha has run out of answers.
Geum gives him one, the ladle glowing over her head. It's this morning's lesson.
His eyes clear. Between the cup, the ice and the tetrapod, it finally makes sense.
So Jaeha lets twenty-eight threads go and trusts Moon Ahin to catch them. She does, on her baton.
The husks crack, but they hold, while she whispers their names.
His load drops from two hundred and ten percent to sixty. His heart steadies.
Then he lays both hands on Borro's back and asks for the next blow, all of it. Borro has heard that before.
Store is ready: thirty seconds of holding, less for a heavier blow. This one will be the heaviest yet.
The Deep Lantern raises her hand higher for the next blow. Far back, Moon Ahin guesses his plan and sends twelve husks sprinting for her flank.
